main_damage_causes: Hannah's independently reasoned sympathy for Harry is slightly flattened by the omission of her concluding rhetorical question, reducing nuance in her moral pushback against the group
Hannah loses her book role as the initiator and driver of the Parseltongue gossip exchange, with her agency transferred to Ernie's expanded film monologue
The corpus is largely faithful — Hannah's core characterization (Hufflepuff, anxious but sympathetic, willing to voice doubt) is preserved in the film, limiting the overall damage

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 73 (Library/Corridor) — Hannah overheard in Hufflepuff conversation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In Book Scene 8, Hannah says 'He always seems so nice, though, and, well, he's the one who made You-Know-Who disappear. He can't be all bad, can he?' — this is an expression of genuine moral uncertainty and independent sympathy for Harry, pushing back against Ernie's certainty with her own reasoning.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hannah's line is condensed to 'He always seems so nice, though. And, after all, he is the one who made You Know Who disappear.' The phrase 'He can't be all bad, can he?' — her tentative but independently reasoned conclusion — is dropped, slightly flattening the beat of her pushing back against the group consensus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version gives Hannah a small but meaningful moment of independent moral reasoning — she is not just noting Harry's niceness but drawing her own tentative conclusion against peer pressure. The film version preserves the general sentiment but loses the concluding rhetorical question, slightly reducing the sense that Hannah is actively resisting the group's narrative rather than merely hedging.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 73 (Library/Corridor) — Ernie's expanded conspiratorial reasoning replaces Hannah's anxious framing
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 6 establishes Hannah as the one who initiates the conversation by asking 'You definitely think it is Potter, then, Ernie?' with anxiety — she is the emotional anchor of the exchange, uncertain and probing. Book Scene 9 notes the Hufflepuffs leaning in together, suggesting a group dynamic Hannah is part of rather than peripheral to.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Hannah is entirely overheard from the corridor — she has no initiating line equivalent to her anxious book question that opens the exchange. Ernie dominates the scene with an expanded conspiratorial monologue (adding details about Filch's cat and Creevey not in the book version of this scene). Hannah's two lines are reactive only, losing her role as the one who frames and drives the inquiry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the books Hannah actively opens and steers this conversation through her questions, giving her a small but real agential role. In the film she is reduced to a passive reactor to Ernie's monologue. The shift transfers conversational agency entirely to Ernie, making Hannah a sounding board rather than a participant, which slightly diminishes her characterization as a curious, independently minded Hufflepuff.
